theme: Abraham’s death; Jacob and Esau; Isaac’s covenant renewed
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 25:1-26:35. The first chapter records Abraham’s death and the birth of Jacob and Esau. The second focuses on Isaac, his struggles with the Philistines, the renewal of the covenant to him, and Esau’s marriage to Hittite women. Watch for how the patterns of Abraham’s life are repeating in Isaac’s.
settingTheScene: Abraham is 175 when he dies, having lived to see Isaac married and the covenant pass to the next generation. After his death, the story narrows to Isaac. Isaac is in many ways the quietest of the patriarchs, there are fewer dramatic episodes in his life than in his father’s or his son’s. But this chapter shows that the covenant continues to operate. Isaac and Rebekah struggle with infertility, just as Abraham and Sarah did. Twins are born, Esau and Jacob. And the same kinds of trials and blessings that marked Abraham’s life now mark Isaac’s.
observation: Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, and has more children, but Isaac alone inherits everything (25:5).
Abraham dies “in a good old age, an old man and full of years”, the first peaceful death in the Bible.
Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham together at Machpelah. Family reconciliation at the grave.
Rebekah is barren for twenty years. Isaac prays for her, and she conceives.
Two nations struggle in Rebekah’s womb. God tells her: “the older shall serve the younger.”
Esau sells his birthright for stew. The text notes: “Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
Genesis 26 echoes Abraham’s life in striking ways: famine, deception about a wife being a sister, conflict over wells.
God renews the covenant to Isaac: “I will multiply your offspring… in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.”
Esau marries two Hittite women, causing grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
interpretation:
Genesis 25 and 26 mark a transition. The Abraham era ends; the Isaac era begins. But the patterns continue. The covenant promises are renewed. The same struggles arise. The same faithfulness of God is displayed.

Abraham’s death is significant in its peacefulness. He is described as dying “in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people.” This is the first instance in Scripture of the phrase “gathered to his people”, language that suggests something more than mere burial, perhaps anticipating the reunion of the patriarchs in the life to come. Abraham’s death is not tragic but full. He has seen the promise begin to be fulfilled, and he dies in peace.

The mention of Ishmael at the burial is touching. Isaac and Ishmael, half-brothers long separated by Sarah’s demand and Hagar’s exile, come together at their father’s grave. Death often brings reconciliation. The covenant blessing passes to Isaac, but the brotherly bond between the two sons is recognized at this moment.

Then attention shifts to Isaac and Rebekah. They have been married for twenty years without children. The pattern of barrenness is repeating, the same struggle Sarah faced. The covenant family seems perpetually on the edge of extinction, and God always answers prayer just in time. Isaac prays. Rebekah conceives.

But the pregnancy is difficult. Twins are wrestling inside her. She inquires of the LORD, and God reveals the future: “Two nations are in your womb… and the older shall serve the younger.” This is the doctrine of election in narrative form. Before either child has done anything good or bad, God has chosen the younger over the older. Paul will pick this up in Romans 9 as a key proof text for God’s sovereign election. The blessing does not flow by birth order. It flows by God’s choice.

Esau and Jacob are born. Esau, the elder, becomes a man of the field, a skilled hunter, his father’s favorite. Jacob, the younger, dwells in tents and is his mother’s favorite. The stage is set for the conflict that will dominate the rest of Genesis.

The famous birthright episode shows the contrast in character. Esau comes in from the field hungry. He sees Jacob’s stew. He demands it. Jacob, calculating and opportunistic, offers it in exchange for the birthright. Esau swears, eats, and goes on his way. The text’s verdict is brief and damning: “Thus Esau despised his birthright.” The blessing of God meant so little to him that he traded it for a meal. Hebrews 12 will hold this up as a warning to believers: do not be like Esau, who sold his blessing for a single meal.

Genesis 26 then echoes Abraham’s life in striking ways. Famine drives Isaac to Gerar, the same place his father went. Isaac lies about Rebekah, calling her his sister, the same lie his father told twice. Abimelech (or his successor) again deals with the patriarch’s deception. Isaac digs wells; the Philistines stop them up; conflict ensues. The patterns are remarkably similar.

But God renews the covenant to Isaac. “I will be with you and will bless you… and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven… and in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.” The promise made to Abraham now belongs to Isaac. The covenant is generational. It does not stop with one person; it is passed to the next.

The chapter ends with a quiet sorrow: Esau marries two Hittite women, against the covenant pattern of marrying within the covenant family. The choices of Esau will have consequences for centuries to come.
connection: The covenant passes from Abraham to Isaac. The same pattern that marked Abraham, barrenness then miraculous birth, famine then provision, deception then divine protection, now marks Isaac. And the line of promise continues to narrow: not all of Isaac’s children, but Jacob in particular, will carry the covenant forward. Romans 9 will return to this chapter to show that God’s saving purposes operate by election, not by ethnic descent.
application:
Two warnings emerge from these chapters. First, do not despise your birthright. Whatever spiritual blessings God has given you, your salvation, your church, your access to Scripture, your privileged knowledge of the gospel, do not trade them for cheap satisfactions. Esau sold his birthright for stew because the stew was tangible and the birthright was not. Watch out for the daily temptation to trade eternal goods for momentary pleasures.

Second, take heart that God is faithful across generations. The covenant did not stop with Abraham. It passed to Isaac. The God who blessed your spiritual parents and grandparents is the God who blesses you, and who will bless your children if you walk in faith. The covenant is generational. Your faithfulness today shapes the spiritual inheritance of those who come after you.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for carrying his covenant across generations to you.
Confess where you have despised something precious for something immediate.
Ask him to help you pass the faith to someone who comes after you.
